en: The Six Mindfulnesses and Five Contemplations for Newly Ordained Bhikṣus (with Preface), compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Yunkan.
Now, the establishment of the Vinaya teachings by the Śākya is like the system of ritual codes (*li*) possessed by the Confucians. If the rites are not complete, the gentleman deems it so.
If one does not become a complete person and does not abide by the laws, the śramaṇa is said to lack the initial resolve.
If these two are cultivated, then the Confucian may attain his goal, and the Śākya may attain his goal.

His Majesty the Emperor, who was formerly granted a prophecy by the Buddha, annually ordains members of the monastic community (the *tzu-wu*), constantly desiring that the Way of the Benevolent One (*Nengren*) and the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius both be spread and protected throughout the world. Those with shaven heads...
Furthermore, how can those who have recently donned the robes fail to be cautious regarding their virtue and fail to exert themselves in pure cultivation?

Moreover, the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and five contemplations (*pañca-vipaśyanā*) are truly the daily routine for a bhikṣu. Yet, there are often those who, upon first receiving full ordination, abandon them and do not practice them;
and there are also those who focus solely on the recitation of words without grounding themselves in their meaning.
Alas! If one does not attain liberation in this very life, there is a genuine fear that by the time one reaches old age, one will have strayed too far from the Way.
For this reason, I have relied upon the Southern Mountains to carry out my practice, selecting and gathering the authentic teachings to provide these annotations.
This is so that those who are new to study may not falter or stumble at the very first step.

The Dharma of the Six Recollections at Dawn is derived from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Every morning at the break of day, one should universally pay homage to the Triple Gem and cultivate the Fivefold Repentance.

Thereafter, one recites the Six Recollections while kneeling alternately with palms joined, personally articulating the words so that they may be heard by the ears. "Six" (ṣaṭ) signifies the number; "recollection" (*smṛti*) clarifies the meaning.
It is recorded as being of the nature [of a lunar day]. Regarding the first thought-moment of knowledge of the sun and moon, one should say:
"Today is the first day of the bright fortnight," up to the fifteenth day; because it is purely large, one does not mention "small" or "large."

If the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is of varying length, it must be divided into two parts: today being the first day of the long dark fortnight up to the fifteenth, or today being the first day of the short dark fortnight up to the fourteenth.
This refers to the method for calculating the distance from the *poṣadha* ceremony when leaving the household life, as well as the reckoning of days and months.
If one follows the Vinaya texts, this is intended for laypeople who inquire about it and have it conveyed.

Regarding the awareness of dates: if one enters a village, one should first determine the number of days according to the lunar calendar, taking into account the specific customs of that region regardless of whether they follow the "black" or "white" reckoning systems.

When answering laypeople, one may only state the general characteristics, saying, "This is the small [intercalary] month; today is such-and-such a day. This way, it will be appropriate for both the monastic and the laity to understand.
Second, regarding the awareness of the place where food is received, there are three cases:
(1) if one entirely declines an invitation, one says, "I shall now eat my own [alms]; (2) if one has already eaten, one says, "I have already eaten";
(3) if one says, "I always eat the regular food of the Saṃgha," or "I always beg for alms. (4) If one accepts an invitation, one says, "I shall now eat my own [alms]."
Regarding "having no invitation" (*apratigrāhaka*): it is said, "I am now eating the food of the *saṃgha and have no invitation," or "I am now begging for alms and have no invitation.

If there is an invitation, one must consider whether there is a transgression (*parihāra*) or not. If there is no transgression, one should say: "There is currently an invitation; I shall go of my own accord.
If there is a transgression, this refers to circumstances such as the *kārttika* month, illness, or the distribution of robes (*cīvara*).

One should say: "Now, due to a certain circumstance, I am able to decline an invitation. If there is no such circumstance and one receives many invitations on a single day, one should formally relinquish the invitations before others, saying:
"Today I have received many invitations; I shall accept one for myself and give the remainder to the Elder [Name] at [Place].
One should seek out a group of five monastics to relinquish them. If there is no one present, one should relinquish them through mental resolve, saying: "I, [Name],..."
This morning, the donor has offered me a proper meal; I now transfer this merit to [Name] Bhikṣu. The donor does not calculate for me that I have received food at will.
(Recite this three times. Third, one should be mindful of the time of receiving the precepts and the number of years since ordination (*varṣāgra*).
"I received full ordination on such-and-such a day, month, year, at such-and-such a time, when the shadow of a one-foot gnomon was such-and-such a length.
I have no *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat) yet; should I have one later, it shall be stated according to the *varṣa*. Now, since in this region the shadow is not measured, one simply says:
'In the year such-and-such, in the cyclical year such-and-such, in the month such-and-such, on the new moon day such-and-such, at such-and-such a time, during the upper, middle, or lower division.'"
Having fulfilled the full precepts, the fourth [recollection] is to know whether one's robes and bowl are present or not, and to perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*).
One says: "I possess my three robes and bowl; having been in excess, I have already performed the purification. Or, if there is a deficiency among the three robes, one says: [as follows].

"I lack such-and-such a robe; I now accept and maintain such-and-such a robe. Furthermore, regarding the regulation on extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), if ten days have passed since they were acquired, one must declare them pure (*śuddhi-ārocana*);
if they have not yet been declared pure, one says, "they have not yet been declared pure.
The fifth mindfulness concerns eating separately from others.
It is said: "If one relies on eating with the assembly, there must be specific conditions for eating separately. This refers to the nine conditions, such as illness, which permit exceptions.
One should say: "I now have such-and-such a condition; I ought to eat separately from the assembly."
The sixth mindfulness concerns physical strength and weakness:

one should reflect, "I am free from illness and capable of practicing the Path," or, if one has an illness, reflect upon its treatment. The Five Contemplations during the time of eating: 1. Contemplate the difficulty of obtaining food. 2. Contemplate the toil involved in producing it. 3. Contemplate the nature of impurity. 4. Contemplate the debt of gratitude toward those who provide it. 5. Contemplate the medicine that sustains life.

However, when one is able to practice the fourfold offerings of clothing, food, shelter, and medicine; when one can give away things while abandoning stinginess, and receive gifts while removing greed—then both subject and object are pure, generating vast merit and great benefit.
For now, we shall establish a contemplation based on the time of eating to open the path of the mind, briefly setting forth five gates as clarified in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
To divide it thus: the Sanskrit term is *vipaśyanā*, which translates into Chinese as "contemplation" (*guān*). This means:
These five types must all involve the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*), associated with wisdom (*prajñā*), to investigate and examine them.
Nowadays, there are those who recite these aloud, which are mocked by those who possess true knowledge. As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:

"If one does not contemplate the nature of food and the mind remains stubbornly attached to its delicious taste, one will fall among the impure worms, with molten copper poured into one's mouth," and so forth. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If [one is] sharp..."

When a practitioner of sharp faculties receives food, they maintain mindfulness at every mouthful (mindfulness being equivalent to contemplation); when receiving clothing, they maintain mindfulness with each garment;
and when entering a room, they maintain mindfulness with each entry. As for those of dull faculties, when first obtaining food, clothing, and lodging, they maintain a single collective mindfulness.
The *Nien-tsang* (Mindfulness Storehouse) says: "Having begged for food from within the village, once obtained, he leaves the village and proceeds to the edge of the water."
In a place suitable for practicing the Way, set aside food on one side and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

One should contemplate that the various foods are loathsome and view one's own body as an utterly foul vessel. It is said that when eating, one must not exceed three spoonfuls, in order to sever all evil.
Taking the first spoonful is for the cultivation of all goodness; taking the middle spoonful is for the deliverance of all sentient beings.
Because it has been produced, one proceeds to take the subsequent spoonfuls, up until the point of dedicating them toward the Buddha-way, and proceeds with the remaining vegetables and so forth.
First, one calculates the amount of labor expended and measures its origin;
as the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "One contemplates this food: its plowing, planting, weeding, harvesting, threshing, grinding, washing, and cooking."
To cook it until it is ready for use requires great effort; calculating it for a single bowl of food, one must exert oneself until sweat flows.
When the food is small but the sweat is vast, it turns foul in an instant. If I were to harbor greed, I would fall into hell to eat glowing iron balls.
Emerging from hell, I would become various kinds of animals to repay my past debts, perhaps as a pig or a dog, constantly eating excrement.

Therefore, one should cultivate a sense of revulsion toward food. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It was said to the bhikṣus: 'Consider this single grain of rice; it is produced through a hundredfold labor.

It represents the portion set aside for one's wife and children, yet it is given as an offering for the sake of merit. How can you then discard it? Furthermore, the *Jingxin jieguan* (Pure Mind Precept Contemplation) says:
'Consider a bowl of food; it produces a bowl of sweat. That sweat resides within the skin and flesh; this is precisely what constitutes that food.'"
The blood required for the effort of preparing a single meal for one person amounts to a bowlful of blood; how much more so for the food consumed throughout an entire lifetime?
From the initial plowing of the fields until the food enters the mouth, countless varieties of small insects are injured and killed.
For this reason, the Buddha’s precept is to sustain one's life and pass through a lifetime by receiving only one meal per day.
Second, one should reflect upon whether one’s own virtuous conduct is complete or deficient, abundant or meager.

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one does not practice seated meditation or recite the scriptures, nor attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, yet accepts the offerings of the faithful, one falls into the sin of misappropriating such gifts.

If one is aware that these three types of activity are absent, yet the donor gives out of knowledge [of this], both parties fall into the sin of misappropriating gifts; the bhikṣu is guilty of being greedily satiated."

If one gives food while harboring a mind of arrogance, or after having eaten oneself, eats excessively to the point of over-saturation for the sake of giving, one falls [into a lower realm] because that food was also obtained from a donor.
For this reason, throughout the long night [of his teaching], the Buddha has always praised the practice of "final-limit eating," which refers to the last reduction of mouthfuls.
If one eats further after already having eaten sufficiently, it does not increase one's physical appearance or strength, but only increases [one's burden].

Because of these afflictions, one should not eat without moderation; furthermore, if one's virtuous precepts are complete, it is permissible to receive much, but if one's virtue is deficient, one should appropriately reduce what is received.
Third, guarding the mind reveals that transgressions do not exceed the three poisons.
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī-ṭīkā* states: In the Vinaya, it is taught that when a renunciant receives food, they must first examine the food before consuming it;

generally, there are three kinds of food. Regarding superior food, which gives rise to craving and should be avoided, there are four matters: first, the fault of attachment to joy and pleasure, because one becomes attached to fragrance and flavor, and though body and mind are at ease, one indulges in sensory gratification;
second, the fault of intoxication by food, after having finished eating... [the body... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the extant portion provided.)*
Third, one is free from the fault of seeking a fine complexion; having finished eating, one delights in a radiant and healthy appearance, and does not require this mind [of attachment].
Fourth, one is free from the fault of seeking bodily adornment; having finished eating, one delights in being well-satisfied and robust.
Second, if one eats with a lowly attitude, aversion and anger will arise, leading mostly to rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*), where one will never see food again.
Third, those who do not distinguish between fine and coarse food, whose minds give rise to much delusion, and who die and fall among the animals to become various worms that feed on excrement,
such as dung-eating insects— by reversing these three poisons, they form the three roots of goodness and are reborn in the three good realms.
The four right efforts are like excellent medicine taken to rescue the body from suffering and eliminate chronic ailments.
By not treating hunger and thirst, one’s spiritual practice is neglected and new illnesses arise.
By reducing and restricting food and drink, previously ingested food is digested. Furthermore, two matters serve as analogies: first, it is like oiling a cart, which merely allows it to turn.

1. Regarding the inquiry as to whether oil is good or bad: when one wishes to cross a perilous road and their child has already died, and being driven by the urgency of hunger and poverty, they eat the flesh of their own child, they must certainly not crave its flavor.
5. To accomplish the work of the Way, worldly retributions are unintended.

There are three general intentions: first, to cause the body to endure for a long time; for the body of the desire realm must rely upon solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), and without it, it cannot endure, leaving the conditions for the Path without a basis.
Second, to ensure the continuity of the life-span; by relying on this retribution-body and its provisional life, one establishes the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).
Third, to cultivate precept, concentration, and wisdom to subdue and extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus one maintains [the body].

The world says that if one does not eliminate the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*), this is the way of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and one is not permitted to receive even a single cup of water from them;
the *Buddha-piṭaka* is likewise. One must certainly loathe the inversion of self and should not give rise to attachment toward coarse food or rag robes.

Furthermore, when obtaining food to sustain the body, it is not for the sake of seeking the fruits of happiness in the realms of humans or devas. As for those who do not exhaust [these attachments], it is as extensively detailed by the Great Master of the Southern Mountain (Dōgen).
The *Xingshichao*, *Jingxinjieguan*, *Jiaojieyi*, and other works clarify this matter.

If one possesses sharp faculties and a quick nature, and applies oneself with earnest devotion to learning from those who have attained the Way, then within a few years, one may enter the abyss of the precepts and prohibitions, reach the treasury of meditative concentration and wisdom, and penetrate the profound depths of the sages and worthies. Were it otherwise, the scriptures...
Yun said: "Since I am neither a man of the Way nor a layman, I have no name. The Confucian says:
'Though there be choice delicacies, if one does not eat them, one will not know their flavor; though there be the ultimate Way, if one does not study it, one will not know its excellence.
Is this not so? Furthermore, the five contemplations issued by the Emperor above differ from those previously printed and circulated; these are based on the authentic text of the Nanshan [Vinaya]."
[This is] also [the case]. Regarding the method for expelling those who have consumed the food (appended note):
Nanshan says that one may chant [the formula] before the meal and expel them once it has been obtained, or after the meal; this is not recorded in the sutras or śāstras.
The text is arranged according to the circumstances: whenever food is produced, it must in every instance be prepared in accordance with the Dharma and must not be mixed with discarded refuse.
In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, after the Buddha had received the precept against killing from the *Kāntāra* (Wilderness) spirit, he addressed the spirit, saying:
"I now command my śrāvaka disciples that wherever the Buddha-dharma exists, they shall all provide you with food; if there is a residence where they are unable to provide it,"
Such persons are merely partisans of the celestial Māra and are not my disciples. Within the monasteries of the fourfold *saṃgha*, shrines for spirits are established;

tradition says that in the monasteries of China, temples for spirits, temples for the *ārāma-devatā*, and temples for Piṇḍola are maintained, and whenever the two daily meals arrive, the monastics send food to these three places.
Other bhikṣus do not go out [to collect it]. This is as commanded in the *Āryā-Mahāprajāpatī-Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra*.
The *Jiaojie yishu* (Exegesis on the Ritual Precepts) states that whatever cakes are produced should be about the size of a fingernail, and rice should not exceed seven grains;
other foods and drinks likewise must not be given in excess. At that time, he recites a verse:

"O assembly of ghosts and spirits, I now bestow this offering upon you: these seven grains pervade the ten directions for all ghosts and spirits. The *Zhilun* (Treatise on Wisdom) also says: [The text continues with the citation from the *Zhilun*.]

When spirits and deities receive a single mouthful of food from a person, they produce a thousandfold or ten-thousandfold return. If one wishes for such a great increase, one must contribute one’s own portion into the permanent endowment (*sthavira-vastu*);

otherwise, one commits the offense of stealing the Sangha’s food. Alternatively, if one has obtained food through begging, it is permissible to practice moderation by reducing one's own share and giving it away.
Thus, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "Whenever one obtains food through begging, divide it into four parts; give one part [to others]."

One-third [of the food] is given to fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life; one-third is given to the destitute and beggars; one-third is given to the various ghosts and spirits; and one-fourth is for one's own sustenance.

Following this principle, if one wishes to extend the mind to universal giving, according to the *Nanyue Shifa* (The Method of Eating at Mount Nanyue) within the *Sui ziyi* (Following One’s Own Intent), it says:
regarding the food obtained, one should say: "May this food—superior in color, fragrance, and flavor—be offered upward to the ten directions."

Within the Buddha-dharma, offerings are made to all the worthy sages above and down to those of the six realms of existence; these gifts are bestowed without discrimination, so that according to their individual capacities, all are fully satisfied.

This causes all donors to attain immeasurable *pāramitās*. Furthermore, it is said that one should contemplate the color and fragrance of the food as being like the sandalwood wind, which at once universally perfumes the worlds of the ten directions.
Whether ordinary or holy beings, each who has a karmic connection receives the supreme flavor, and those in the six realms likewise hear [the scent].
Arousing the bodhicitta while eating can give rise to the six pāramitās; such a mental application is truly great.

Furthermore, in the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*, it is recorded that when the Buddha and the great assembly were given poisoned medicine, the Buddha had them chant "traipittaka" before consuming it, whereby all the poison was transformed into delicious food; this is indeed a secret teaching. Moreover, it should be...
Know that food possesses three virtues and six flavors. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the three virtues are: first, lightness and softness; second, purity and cleanliness;
third, conformity to the Dharma. The six flavors are: first, bitter; second, sour; third, sweet; fourth, pungent; fifth, salty; sixth, bland.
Those who have newly entered the Path must strive to understand these quickly; exert yourselves, exert yourselves!
The Six Mindfulnesses and Five Contemplations for Newly Ordained Bhikṣus (End)
